bull_bear.body: The **INR 10,150 cr raise — the largest growth capital raise in the Indian power sector** — came in three parts: INR 3,000 cr promoter preferential (INR 1,125 cr received, INR 1,875 cr due before June 2027), INR 3,150 cr from selling 2.5 cr of 7 cr JSW Steel shares, and a INR 4,000 cr QIP. Result: INR 12,880 cr cash, leverage 4.95x from 5.2x, and enough to fund the equity portion of the INR 20,000 cr FY27 capex plus 2030 growth plans. FY27 funding maths given openly: ~INR 12,000-12,500 cr from raise plus operating cash; the balance to INR 20,000 cr is incremental debt (implying roughly INR 7,500 cr). Inorganic activity continues selectively (Maruti Clean Coal, GE boilers, TJPS stake-up, KSK 26% call option). Discipline signal: skipped the SECI pumped-hydro tender on a clearance technicality rather than stretching, and will only enter merchant BESS "when it makes sense that our benchmark returns are protected."
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
- **PAT/ROE suppression persists** — the honest answer given was 4-5 years per asset for EBITDA-to-PAT translation. With ~3 GW/yr of additions, the drag is structural, not transitory.
- **TGNA curtailment**: 700 MW total (300 MW + 400 MW O2 Rajasthan) currently exposed; one conversion promised by 31-Aug, the other slipped to Sep/Oct.
- **Hydrology volatility** — a 26% portfolio generation decline on basin-level weakness (Sutlej −39%) with no company-specific mitigation beyond capacity charges.
- **Chinese equipment dependency** for the Mahanadi 4th unit, and **no long-term cell supply partnership** for BESS ("Right now, no") — warranties sit with the OEM cell maker.
- **Leverage stays high** at ~4.95x with a 2030 target of merely "below 5 times" — this is a levered compounder by design.
- Net debt of ~INR 55,000 cr against INR 3,103 cr of quarterly EBITDA; interest at INR 1,519 cr consumes roughly half of EBITDA.
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: Detailed and numerate, with a strong bias to giving checkable specifics — plant-level PLF explanations, the exact seasonal solar PLF curve, the funding bridge arithmetic, the BESS margin in $/kWh, the curtailment revenue impact in rupees. Where they declined (project-level pumped-hydro capex, FY28 guidance) they said so and committed to a date. The CEO was willing to accept an analyst's INR 5 cr/MW benchmark rather than dodge it ("Not very far from this number"). Notably, every softer PLF number was explained with a specific, verifiable cause (planned shutdown, force majeure, basin hydrology) rather than generic macro. The one area of visible reticence is Mahanadi units 5-6 and FY28, both deferred to "the right time very soon."
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body:
- **The flat P&L is the intended output of the strategy, not a failure of it.** 1,558 MW of YoY additions produced zero revenue growth because generation fell on hydrology and planned outages, while depreciation and interest fully capitalised. Investors modelling EBITDA growth off capacity growth will keep being wrong for several more quarters.
- **Curtailment is nearly costless where GNA exists.** 69 MU of curtailment cost only ~INR 15 cr because GNA backdowns are deemed availability — the tariff is still earned. The real exposure is confined to the two TGNA projects.
- **JSW is now an equipment manufacturer that happens to own power plants.** With TJPS at 2x800 TG and GE Durgapur heading to 1.6 GW of boilers, it controls the scarcest input in Indian thermal — and management explicitly said this covers "both our current projects and future opportunities," i.e. potential third-party sales optionality.
- **Buyers are actively preferring 600 MW and smaller units** because deeper backdown at 50% is easier with high solar penetration — a demand-side quirk that makes Mahanadi's 600 MW unit easier to tie up than a 800 MW block.
- Pumped hydro's "significantly high-teen IRRs" against a mid-teen corporate benchmark is the highest-return asset class management named on the call, and 3,000 MW of it is already PPA-contracted.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- ₹10,150 Cr raised for growth and deleveraging: ₹4,000 Cr QIP (25th May), ₹3,150 Cr gross proceeds from partial JSW Steel stake sale (2.5 Cr of 7 Cr shares, 18th May) and ₹3,000 Cr preferential allotment to promoters (₹1,125 Cr received; balance before June 2027).
- Net debt ₹61,322 Cr at Jun-26 (TTM net leverage 5.53x), split operational net debt ₹54,885 Cr and CWIP net debt ₹6,437 Cr; ND/Equity fell to 1.70x from 2.15x at Mar-26.
- Operational net leverage (ND excl. CWIP / EBITDA, TTM) improved to 4.95x — the deck describes this as improving "from ~5.2x (TTM) in FY26" while the chart shows 5.23x at Mar-26.
- Cash & cash equivalents of ₹12,881 Cr, described as sufficient with "future internal accruals to fund equity portion of estimated Capex till FY30 (~₹1.1 trillion)".
- Cash Return on Adjusted Net Worth fell to 14% (TTM Jun-26) from 18% at Mar-26, which the deck attributes to the QIP raising net worth (adjusted net worth ₹31,336 Cr vs ₹23,781 Cr).

bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Renewable energy intermittency — Solar, wind and hydro output is inherently intermittent; the report positions the thermal fleet as providing 'critical baseload support and grid stability, particularly during peak demand and renewable intermittency,' implying structural reliance on thermal capacity to offset this gap as the renewable share of the portfolio grows.
- Rising leverage from debt-funded growth — Net debt gearing rose to 0.59 times at the end of FY2025-26 from 0.39 times a year earlier, reflecting increased debt used to fund capacity growth and acquisitions.
- Supply chain dependence — The Company frames its expansion into green hydrogen, battery assembly and backward-integrated manufacturing as steps to 'enhance competitiveness and reduce supply chain dependence,' implying the existing thermal/renewable equipment supply chain carries dependency risk that these initiatives are intended to mitigate.
- Macro, geopolitical and climate volatility — The Company's own framing cites navigating 'a changing energy landscape and increasing energy demands, climate challenges, and evolving geopolitical realities' as a condition it must manage, indicating exposure to macro, policy and climate-related uncertainty affecting its long-dated generation assets.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body:
- **Thermal (5.7 GW):** generation −6% YoY to 8 BU. Open capacity now **under 4%**. API4 coal index rose from $90 to $113 (+25%) YoY but the domestic-coal shift kept the portfolio resilient. Mahanadi's 85% annual plant-availability entitlement means fixed-charge income is recognised now with cash collection over the following 2-3 quarters.
- **Hydro:** capacity up (Tidong + Kutehr) but generation −26% on a late snowmelt and long winter. July recovery is strong — Karcham, Baspa and Kutehr all running above 100% PLF; management expects design energy for the full year and continues to earn capacity charges regardless.
- **RE:** solar generation +29%, wind +3% on 1,168 MW of added capacity. Q1 solar PLF 21% — management gave the seasonal shape explicitly: **Q1 ~22%, Q2 lower, Q3 26%, Q4 28%, annualised ~25%.** July wind PLF already 5-6% above June.
- **Equipment manufacturing:** TJPS stake raised from 2.4% to **10.7%**; Halol blade plant commissioned; 5 GWh BESS plant trials complete and supplying.
business.title: Segment / subsidiary detail

business.body:
- **Integration speed on acquisitions:** Tidong was acquired in January 2026 and commissioned by Q1 FY27 — four months ahead of its October 2026 schedule. Management framed this as "a testament to the integration capabilities our teams bring to every acquisition."
- **Equipment supply-chain control** — the TJPS + GE boiler combination removes the single biggest execution constraint on 800 MW-class thermal in India.
- **Merchant exposure under 4%** with fixed-cost recovery even during backdowns — "we continue to recover our fixed costs in these kinds of backdowns. We are not kind of impacted."
- **Mine-mouth thermal cost position:** the Mahanadi 4th unit will be built "significantly lower than the benchmark per MW cost of capacity addition" and sits next to the mine — attractive on merchant *or* PPA.
- **Technical-minimum resilience:** while the industry runs below technical minimum during the midday solar peak, Utkal never went below 58-60% PLF and the fleet ran >85% PLF / >90% availability in July; capability to run below 50% already demonstrated at Ratnagiri and Vijayanagar.

latest_quarter.body: EBITDA grew only 2% on flat revenue because generation fell 5% (hydrology + planned shutdowns + one-off Mahanadi evacuation) even as capacity rose 1,558 MW. Coal cost pressure was real (API4 +25% YoY) but blunted by the domestic-coal shift. The structural margin issue is below EBITDA: depreciation +20% and interest +16% as new assets capitalise, with interest charged to P&L staying elevated in the initial years because the construction-period moratorium ends at COD. Management's stated normalisation path is **4-5 years per asset** before EBITDA translates properly into PBT/PAT — an explicitly industry-wide mechanic, not a JSW-specific problem. Merchant tailwind is genuine: DAM prices rose from ~INR 4.40/unit in Q1 FY26 to **INR 5.10/unit in Q1 FY27 (+16%)**, against an FY26 average of INR 3.86.

- **FY27: 3 GW capacity addition and INR 20,000 cr capex — "firmly on track"**, with ~36% of the capacity guidance already achieved by the call date.

- **Net leverage below 5.0x by 2030** — a committed target; already at 4.95x.
- **Salboni Phase 1 (2x800 MW):** supplier deliveries and commissioning "in line with the PPA timelines"; TG order placed with TJPS, civil order placed, site work in full swing, 100% land acquired, all key clearances received.
- **Mahanadi 4th unit (600 MW): commissioning in FY28**, on track, orders placed and material under dispatch (Chinese suppliers, with import permission received). Units 5 and 6 (taking 1.8 → 3.6 GW) — strategy announcement "at the right time very soon".
- **Mahanadi doubling capex to be "at least 25% to 30% lower" per MW than the Salboni greenfield benchmark.**
- **GE Durgapur boiler acquisition to complete "by end of this quarter" (Q2 FY27)** — nameplate 1.1 GW, taken to **1.6 GW (2x800) with de-bottlenecking and minor investment** already planned, to match TJPS Chennai's 2x800 TG capacity.
- **Chitradurga wind-blade facility: commissioning by FY27** (Halol already commissioned 8-Jun-2026, 450 blades/yr ≈ 600 MW of installations).
- **BESS: ~INR 150 cr of annual EBITDA from the 5 GWh plant** at full running, on ~$15 mn of annual revenue at $2.75-3.00/kWh assembly margin. First large external order of **~INR 440 cr** received.
- **Pumped hydro: "significantly high-teen IRRs"** (vs the mid-teen benchmark), with capex "not very far from" INR 5 cr/MW. Bhavali (1,500 MW, MSEDCL PPA) fully ready — EC received, land majority acquired, forest Stage-1 received, civil order to L&T, electromechanical to Voith. Kandhaura (1,680 MW, 1,500 MW PPA with UP) — **readiness to start execution by the last quarter of FY27.**
- **TGNA→GNA conversions:** 300 MW currently curtailed "almost certain… before 31st August"; the 400 MW O2 Power Rajasthan project connectivity slipped from July-end to **September or October**.
- **KSK Mahanadi:** call option notice already issued on the remaining 26% stake — minority outflow to shrink substantially on close.
- **Funding of FY27 capex:** ~INR 7,000 cr raised plus operating cash gives ~INR 12,000-12,500 cr; the balance to INR 20,000 cr is the incremental debt requirement. **INR 1,875 cr of promoter preferential capital still to come** (last date June 2027).

- A further **~9 GWh pumped-hydro site is now ready** for future tenders (JSW skipped the recent SECI tender solely because forest Stage-1 clearance was a pre-condition it could not meet at any other site).
- **BESS: first large external order ~INR 440 cr** (200 MW / 400 MWh equivalent), plus small third-party supplies already delivered.
- **Maruti Clean Coal & Power (300 MW, Chhattisgarh):** definitive agreement signed. 195 MW net long-term PPA with Rajasthan discoms, 14 years residual PPA life; 5% at variable cost to Chhattisgarh discom; ~64 MW merchant. Coal via long-term SECL FSA + SHAKTI linkage.

outlook.body:
- **Vertical integration is now essentially complete for the thermal build-out** — "we are totally de-risked in terms of the supply chain of boiler, turbine, generators for all our 800 MW expansion plants." TJPS Chennai 2x800 TG + GE Durgapur boiler at 1.6 GW post-debottlenecking.
- **BESS backward integration:** in discussion with technology partners to make cells in India rather than import, and to scale the container from 5 MWh to 6/7/8 MWh for better cost efficiency. Government PLI for cells is being evaluated.
- **Merchant BESS:** not yet, but actively explored — the logic given is compelling (existing solar sites, existing connectivity reusable post-solar-hours, DC-side-only solar capex to charge the battery, and thermal evening-peak capacity still years away).
- **Maruti Clean Coal brownfield:** management confirmed the option to "double the capacity or even more in the same plant" next to the coal mine.
- Mahanadi units 5 and 6 (1.8 → 3.6 GW) — announcement pending.

outlook.body:
- Strategy 3.0 aims to scale through a balanced portfolio of thermal and greenfield renewable energy assets, energy storage, and energy products & services, with a disciplined focus on delivering strong returns.
- Calibrated capacity addition pursued via both organic build-out and inorganic acquisitions (e.g., Mahanadi, O2 Power, Tidong hydro), validated by a track record of disciplined acquisition and integration.
- Backward integration into thermal and renewable manufacturing (turbine JV with Toshiba, wind turbine technology licensing with SANY, wind blade manufacturing, battery assembly, boiler facility) to strengthen supply-chain resilience, cost competitiveness and execution certainty.
- Building pumped hydro and battery energy storage capacity as a long-duration storage solution to manage demand peaks that solar alone cannot serve.
- Pioneering green hydrogen production as a new decarbonisation pathway, positioned as the start of a scalable clean energy value chain rather than an experiment.
- Digital transformation - embedding artificial intelligence, IoT and data analytics across operations, anchored by a centralised Command Centre in Mumbai for real-time visibility, predictive maintenance and performance optimisation.
- Disciplined capital allocation framework applying a minimum mid-teen IRR threshold to capex decisions while working toward a target net leverage below 5x by FY2030.
- Maintaining a portfolio tilt toward clean energy (targeting ~70% renewables / ~30% thermal by 2030) while retaining thermal capacity as a stable baseload backbone for grid stability.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: JSW Energy's 'Strategy 3.0' targets 30 GW of generation capacity and 40 GWh of energy storage capacity by 2030 (a ~20% CAGR in installed capacity), with the incremental capacity mix skewed toward renewables (~70% renewable / ~30% thermal by 2030). Total locked-in capacity at full built-up stands at 32.1 GW (Thermal 10,658 MW; Wind 6,009 MW; Hybrid 7,110 MW; Hydro 1,781 MW; Solar 6,505 MW), split by end-use as Utility Scale 26,012 MW, Group Captive/C&I 5,396 MW and Merchant 655 MW. As of 31 March 2026, 14,048 MW was under construction or with PPA signed (Thermal 3,200 MW / Wind 2,353 MW / Solar 3,547 MW / Hybrid 4,798 MW / Hydro 150 MW), taking installed-plus-under-construction capacity to 27,502 MW. In FY2026 the company added 2.6 GW of capacity through disciplined organic execution and selective inorganic acquisitions, and completed vertical integration milestones including commissioning of a green hydrogen facility (3,800 TPA capacity) and a battery assembly plant (5 GWh). Strategic thermal growth was anchored via the 3,200 MW Salboni project backed by a PPA, with supply chain de-risked through partnerships and JVs. Key inorganic pursuits in FY2026 included completion of the largest acquisition to date - the 4.7 GW O2 Power renewable energy platform (via JSW Neo Energy), of which ~1.34 GW of operational capacity was acquired in April 2025 and had grown to ~2 GW operational by March 2026 - plus the acquisition of the 150 MW Tidong Hydro Power project, reinforcing the company's position as the largest private hydro player in India. Growth was further supported by a Rs 3,000 crore preferential equity allotment to the Promoter Group to accelerate execution.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- FY2026 demand growth for India's power sector moderated to 0.9%, but peak demand continued to reach new highs (~245 GW in January 2026), and a strong rebound from late Q4 FY2026 into April-May 2026 (all-time peak of 271 GW in May 2026) signals a clear inflection in the demand cycle, not a seasonal spike.
- Electricity demand is projected to grow at 6.4% annually over the next decade, driven by 'Make in India' manufacturing corridors, AI-driven data centre investments, accelerated transport electrification, and rising household consumption.
- Government commitment to 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030, alongside a revised target of 97 GW of incremental thermal capacity by FY2035, implies India will pursue both clean and reliable energy simultaneously.
- The global energy crisis exposed risks of over-reliance on imported fuel and premature retirement of dispatchable capacity, reinforcing energy self-reliance (Atmanirbharta) as a strategic necessity; the path forward combines domestic coal for near-term security, scaled-up renewables, and pumped hydro storage for system flexibility.
- Grid stability and peak demand management cannot be addressed by intermittent renewables alone; domestic thermal power is described as the indispensable bridge enabling industrial growth without compromising reliability.
- Operating-context macro backdrop: world economic growth estimated at 3.4% in CY2025 and India economic growth estimated at 7.7% in FY2026, against India's 500 GW renewable capacity target by FY2030 versus current installed renewables capacity of 274.7 GW.
- Total locked-in generation capacity stands at 32.1 GW, comprising 13.5 GW operational, 14.0 GW under active construction, and 4.6 GW in development.
- Locked-in energy storage capacity stands at 29.6 GWh, comprising 26.4 GWh through pumped hydro and 3.2 GWh through battery systems, with Energy Storage Agreements already secured for the pumped hydro portion.
- MoU pipeline with multiple states for long-duration pumped hydro storage aggregates approximately 80 GWh beyond the projects already under Energy Storage Agreements.

deepdive.thesis: Operationally a landmark quarter — 873 MW added in Q1 and ~1.1 GW since April (36% of the 3 GW FY27 target already banked), Tidong Hydro commissioned four months early, and a INR 10,150 cr capital raise completed that leaves INR 12,880 cr of cash and net leverage down to 4.95x from 5.2x. Financially it looks flat: revenue INR 5,437 cr flat YoY, EBITDA +2%, PAT down — because depreciation (+20%) and interest (+16%) capitalise ahead of the earnings from newly commissioned RE assets, a mechanic management says takes 4-5 years to translate into PBT/PAT. The equity story is therefore entirely about execution against the 3 GW / INR 20,000 cr FY27 plan and the vertical-integration build-out, not about this quarter's P&L.

The Company's own framing cites navigating 'a changing energy landscape and increasing energy demands, climate challenges, and evolving geopolitical realities' as a condition it must manage, indicating exposure to macro, policy and climate-related uncertainty affecting its long-dated generation assets.

currentContext.mdna: FY2026 demand growth for India's power sector moderated to 0.9%, but peak demand continued to reach new highs (~245 GW in January 2026), and a strong rebound from late Q4 FY2026 into April-May 2026 (all-time peak of 271 GW in May 2026) signals a clear inflection in the demand cycle, not a seasonal spike.|Electricity demand is projected to grow at 6.4% annually over the next decade, driven by 'Make in India' manufacturing corridors, AI-driven data centre investments, accelerated transport electrification, and rising household consumption.|Government commitment to 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030, alongside a revised target of 97 GW of incremental thermal capacity by FY2035, implies India will pursue both clean and reliable energy simultaneously.|The global energy crisis exposed risks of over-reliance on imported fuel and premature retirement of dispatchable capacity, reinforcing energy self-reliance (Atmanirbharta) as a strategic necessity; the path forward combines domestic coal for near-term security, scaled-up renewables, and pumped hydro storage for system flexibility.|Grid stability and peak demand management cannot be addressed by intermittent renewables alone; domestic thermal power is described as the indispensable bridge enabling industrial growth without compromising reliability.|Operating-context macro backdrop: world economic growth estimated at 3.4% in CY2025 and India economic growth estimated at 7.7% in FY2026, against India's 500 GW renewable capacity target by FY2030 versus current installed renewables capacity of 274.7 GW.|Total locked-in generation capacity stands at 32.1 GW, comprising 13.5 GW operational, 14.0 GW under active construction, and 4.6 GW in development.|Locked-in energy storage capacity stands at 29.6 GWh, comprising 26.4 GWh through pumped hydro and 3.2 GWh through battery systems, with Energy Storage Agreements already secured for the pumped hydro portion.|MoU pipeline with multiple states for long-duration pumped hydro storage aggregates approximately 80 GWh beyond the projects already under Energy Storage Agreements.

risks.note: Solar, wind and hydro output is inherently intermittent; the report positions the thermal fleet as providing 'critical baseload support and grid stability, particularly during peak demand and renewable intermittency,' implying structural reliance on thermal capacity to offset this gap as the renewable share of the portfolio grows.
Net debt gearing rose to 0.59 times at the end of FY2025-26 from 0.39 times a year earlier, reflecting increased debt used to fund capacity growth and acquisitions.

The Company frames its expansion into green hydrogen, battery assembly and backward-integrated manufacturing as steps to 'enhance competitiveness and reduce supply chain dependence,' implying the existing thermal/renewable equipment supply chain carries dependency risk that these initiatives are intended to mitigate.

The Company's own framing cites navigating 'a changing energy landscape and increasing energy demands, climate challenges, and evolving geopolitical realities' as a condition it must manage, indicating exposure to macro, policy and climate-related uncertainty affecting its long-dated generation assets.

one-line thesis: Operationally a landmark quarter — 873 MW added in Q1 and ~1.1 GW since April (36% of the 3 GW FY27 target already banked), Tidong Hydro commissioned four months early, and a INR 10,150 cr capital raise completed that leaves INR 12,880 cr of cash and net leverage down to 4.95x from 5.2x. Financially it looks flat: revenue INR 5,437 cr flat YoY, EBITDA +2%, PAT down — because depreciation (+20%) and interest (+16%) capitalise ahead of the earnings from newly commissioned RE assets, a mechanic management says takes 4-5 years to translate into PBT/PAT. The equity story is therefore entirely about execution against the 3 GW / INR 20,000 cr FY27 plan and the vertical-integration build-out, not about this quarter's P&L.

| EBITDA | INR 3,103 cr | +2% | Generation down offset by tariffs/mix |
| PAT | INR 533 cr (attributable INR 471 cr) | down YoY | Higher capitalisation of new assets |
| Depreciation | INR 890 cr | +20% | Tracks capacity commissioning |
| Interest | INR 1,519 cr | +16% | Construction-period moratorium ends at COD |

| Cash RoNW (ex-JSW Steel stake) | ~14% | down YoY | Purely from the fundraise-inflated net worth |
> **Adjustments / one-offs:** Tidong Hydro's early commissioning added an incremental **INR 20-22 cr to Q1 EBITDA**. Mahanadi lost ~184 MU (−7% YoY) to a 17-day one-off evacuation-availability issue now fully normalised and to be classified under Force Majeure. Utkal's lower PLF was a *deliberate* planned shutdown to secure annual availability post-PPA — July availability is back above 91%. Utkal's generation was similar YoY but sold under long-term contracts instead of merchant. Curtailment cost 69 MU across wind+solar, worth only **~INR 15 cr** of revenue because GNA-connected backdowns are treated as deemed availability and still earn tariff. RE portfolio comparison is flattered/hurt by hydrology: national hydro −7%, Sutlej basin −39%, Ravi basin −24%.
guidance (critical — verify next quarter:
- **FY27: 3 GW capacity addition and INR 20,000 cr capex — "firmly on track"**, with ~36% of the capacity guidance already achieved by the call date.
- **All 1.9 GW of remaining FY27 capacity is "100% secured from connectivity and which is all commissioned also"** — >530 MW of it is group-captive/off-grid on a dedicated line (fully insulated from grid curtailment), the rest a mix of STU/CTU with connectivity already in place.
- **FY28: capacity addition "in the same range" (~3 GW)**; formal FY28 guidance deferred — "very soon, we will come back for FY28 also."
- **Net leverage below 5.0x by 2030** — a committed target; already at 4.95x.
- **Salboni Phase 1 (2x800 MW):** supplier deliveries and commissioning "in line with the PPA timelines"; TG order placed with TJPS, civil order placed, site work in full swing, 100% land acquired, all key clearances received.
- **Mahanadi 4th unit (600 MW): commissioning in FY28**, on track, orders placed and material under dispatch (Chinese suppliers, with import permission received). Units 5 and 6 (taking 1.8 → 3.6 GW) — strategy announcement "at the right time very soon".
- **Mahanadi doubling capex to be "at least 25% to 30% lower" per MW than the Salboni greenfield benchmark.**
- **GE Durgapur boiler acquisition to complete "by end of this quarter" (Q2 FY27)** — nameplate 1.1 GW, taken to **1.6 GW (2x800) with de-bottlenecking and minor investment** already planned, to match TJPS Chennai's 2x800 TG capacity.
- **Chitradurga wind-blade facility: commissioning by FY27** (Halol already commissioned 8-Jun-2026, 450 blades/yr ≈ 600 MW of installations).
- **BESS: ~INR 150 cr of annual EBITDA from the 5 GWh plant** at full running, on ~$15 mn of annual revenue at $2.75-3.00/kWh assembly margin. First large external order of **~INR 440 cr** received.
- **Pumped hydro: "significantly high-teen IRRs"** (vs the mid-teen benchmark), with capex "not very far from" INR 5 cr/MW. Bhavali (1,500 MW, MSEDCL PPA) fully ready — EC received, land majority acquired, forest Stage-1 received, civil order to L&T, electromechanical to Voith. Kandhaura (1,680 MW, 1,500 MW PPA with UP) — **readiness to start execution by the last quarter of FY27.**
- **TGNA→GNA conversions:** 300 MW currently curtailed "almost certain… before 31st August"; the 400 MW O2 Power Rajasthan project connectivity slipped from July-end to **September or October**.
- **KSK Mahanadi:** call option notice already issued on the remaining 26% stake — minority outflow to shrink substantially on close.
- **Funding of FY27 capex:** ~INR 7,000 cr raised plus operating cash gives ~INR 12,000-12,500 cr; the balance to INR 20,000 cr is the incremental debt requirement. **INR 1,875 cr of promoter preferential capital still to come** (last date June 2027).
order book & pipeline:
- **1.9 GW of FY27 RE capacity remaining to commission**, fully connectivity-secured.
- **Contracted pumped hydro: 3,000 MW of PPAs signed** (Bhavali 1,500 MW with MSEDCL; Kandhaura 1,500 MW of 1,680 MW with UP). **Narihalla, Karnataka** — letter received, local clearances at an advanced stage, PPA expected soon.
- A further **~9 GWh pumped-hydro site is now ready** for future tenders (JSW skipped the recent SECI tender solely because forest Stage-1 clearance was a pre-condition it could not meet at any other site).
- **BESS: first large external order ~INR 440 cr** (200 MW / 400 MWh equivalent), plus small third-party supplies already delivered.
- **Maruti Clean Coal & Power (300 MW, Chhattisgarh):** definitive agreement signed. 195 MW net long-term PPA with Rajasthan discoms, 14 years residual PPA life; 5% at variable cost to Chhattisgarh discom; ~64 MW merchant. Coal via long-term SECL FSA + SHAKTI linkage.
segment / subsidiary detail:
- **Thermal (5.7 GW):** generation −6% YoY to 8 BU. Open capacity now **under 4%**. API4 coal index rose from $90 to $113 (+25%) YoY but the domestic-coal shift kept the portfolio resilient. Mahanadi's 85% annual plant-availability entitlement means fixed-charge income is recognised now with cash collection over the following 2-3 quarters.
- **Hydro:** capacity up (Tidong + Kutehr) but generation −26% on a late snowmelt and long winter. July recovery is strong — Karcham, Baspa and Kutehr all running above 100% PLF; management expects design energy for the full year and continues to earn capacity charges regardless.
- **RE:** solar generation +29%, wind +3% on 1,168 MW of added capacity. Q1 solar PLF 21% — management gave the seasonal shape explicitly: **Q1 ~22%, Q2 lower, Q3 26%, Q4 28%, annualised ~25%.** July wind PLF already 5-6% above June.
- **Equipment manufacturing:** TJPS stake raised from 2.4% to **10.7%**; Halol blade plant commissioned; 5 GWh BESS plant trials complete and supplying.
growth verticals / optionality:
- **Vertical integration is now essentially complete for the thermal build-out** — "we are totally de-risked in terms of the supply chain of boiler, turbine, generators for all our 800 MW expansion plants." TJPS Chennai 2x800 TG + GE Durgapur boiler at 1.6 GW post-debottlenecking.
- **BESS backward integration:** in discussion with technology partners to make cells in India rather than import, and to scale the container from 5 MWh to 6/7/8 MWh for better cost efficiency. Government PLI for cells is being evaluated.
- **Merchant BESS:** not yet, but actively explored — the logic given is compelling (existing solar sites, existing connectivity reusable post-solar-hours, DC-side-only solar capex to charge the battery, and thermal evening-peak capacity still years away).
- **Maruti Clean Coal brownfield:** management confirmed the option to "double the capacity or even more in the same plant" next to the coal mine.
- Mahanadi units 5 and 6 (1.8 → 3.6 GW) — announcement pending.
6a. moat & competitive position:
- **Integration speed on acquisitions:** Tidong was acquired in January 2026 and commissioned by Q1 FY27 — four months ahead of its October 2026 schedule. Management framed this as "a testament to the integration capabilities our teams bring to every acquisition."
- **Equipment supply-chain control** — the TJPS + GE boiler combination removes the single biggest execution constraint on 800 MW-class thermal in India.
- **Merchant exposure under 4%** with fixed-cost recovery even during backdowns — "we continue to recover our fixed costs in these kinds of backdowns. We are not kind of impacted."
- **Mine-mouth thermal cost position:** the Mahanadi 4th unit will be built "significantly lower than the benchmark per MW cost of capacity addition" and sits next to the mine — attractive on merchant *or* PPA.
- **Technical-minimum resilience:** while the industry runs below technical minimum during the midday solar peak, Utkal never went below 58-60% PLF and the fleet ran >85% PLF / >90% availability in July; capability to run below 50% already demonstrated at Ratnagiri and Vijayanagar.
margins & cost dynamics: EBITDA grew only 2% on flat revenue because generation fell 5% (hydrology + planned shutdowns + one-off Mahanadi evacuation) even as capacity rose 1,558 MW. Coal cost pressure was real (API4 +25% YoY) but blunted by the domestic-coal shift. The structural margin issue is below EBITDA: depreciation +20% and interest +16% as new assets capitalise, with interest charged to P&L staying elevated in the initial years because the construction-period moratorium ends at COD. Management's stated normalisation path is **4-5 years per asset** before EBITDA translates properly into PBT/PAT — an explicitly industry-wide mechanic, not a JSW-specific problem. Merchant tailwind is genuine: DAM prices rose from ~INR 4.40/unit in Q1 FY26 to **INR 5.10/unit in Q1 FY27 (+16%)**, against an FY26 average of INR 3.86.
capex / expansion (watch slippage):
- **On track / ahead:** Tidong (4 months early), Halol blade plant (commissioned 8-Jun), 5 GWh BESS plant (commissioned Q4 FY26, trials complete), 1.1 GW of the 3 GW FY27 target, Salboni Phase 1 site work, Mahanadi 4th unit for FY28.
- **Explicit slippage to track:** the **400 MW O2 Power Rajasthan connectivity moved from July-end to September/October** — this project stays curtailed under TGNA until then. The separate 300 MW under TGNA is guided to convert "before 31st August."
- **Deferred disclosure:** FY28 guidance; pumped-hydro project-level capex; Mahanadi units 5 and 6 strategy; Narihalla PPA signature.
- **No deferrals** despite geopolitics — "there's no question of any deferral of capacity addition."
capital allocation: The **INR 10,150 cr raise — the largest growth capital raise in the Indian power sector** — came in three parts: INR 3,000 cr promoter preferential (INR 1,125 cr received, INR 1,875 cr due before June 2027), INR 3,150 cr from selling 2.5 cr of 7 cr JSW Steel shares, and a INR 4,000 cr QIP. Result: INR 12,880 cr cash, leverage 4.95x from 5.2x, and enough to fund the equity portion of the INR 20,000 cr FY27 capex plus 2030 growth plans. FY27 funding maths given openly: ~INR 12,000-12,500 cr from raise plus operating cash; the balance to INR 20,000 cr is incremental debt (implying roughly INR 7,500 cr). Inorganic activity continues selectively (Maruti Clean Coal, GE boilers, TJPS stake-up, KSK 26% call option). Discipline signal: skipped the SECI pumped-hydro tender on a clearance technicality rather than stretching, and will only enter merchant BESS "when it makes sense that our benchmark returns are protected."
risks & watch-items:
- **PAT/ROE suppression persists** — the honest answer given was 4-5 years per asset for EBITDA-to-PAT translation. With ~3 GW/yr of additions, the drag is structural, not transitory.
- **TGNA curtailment**: 700 MW total (300 MW + 400 MW O2 Rajasthan) currently exposed; one conversion promised by 31-Aug, the other slipped to Sep/Oct.
- **Hydrology volatility** — a 26% portfolio generation decline on basin-level weakness (Sutlej −39%) with no company-specific mitigation beyond capacity charges.
- **Chinese equipment dependency** for the Mahanadi 4th unit, and **no long-term cell supply partnership** for BESS ("Right now, no") — warranties sit with the OEM cell maker.
- **Leverage stays high** at ~4.95x with a 2030 target of merely "below 5 times" — this is a levered compounder by design.
- Net debt of ~INR 55,000 cr against INR 3,103 cr of quarterly EBITDA; interest at INR 1,519 cr consumes roughly half of EBITDA.
management quality / tone: Detailed and numerate, with a strong bias to giving checkable specifics — plant-level PLF explanations, the exact seasonal solar PLF curve, the funding bridge arithmetic, the BESS margin in $/kWh, the curtailment revenue impact in rupees. Where they declined (project-level pumped-hydro capex, FY28 guidance) they said so and committed to a date. The CEO was willing to accept an analyst's INR 5 cr/MW benchmark rather than dodge it ("Not very far from this number"). Notably, every softer PLF number was explained with a specific, verifiable cause (planned shutdown, force majeure, basin hydrology) rather than generic macro. The one area of visible reticence is Mahanadi units 5-6 and FY28, both deferred to "the right time very soon."
non-obvious takeaways:
- **The flat P&L is the intended output of the strategy, not a failure of it.** 1,558 MW of YoY additions produced zero revenue growth because generation fell on hydrology and planned outages, while depreciation and interest fully capitalised. Investors modelling EBITDA growth off capacity growth will keep being wrong for several more quarters.
- **Curtailment is nearly costless where GNA exists.** 69 MU of curtailment cost only ~INR 15 cr because GNA backdowns are deemed availability — the tariff is still earned. The real exposure is confined to the two TGNA projects.
- **JSW is now an equipment manufacturer that happens to own power plants.** With TJPS at 2x800 TG and GE Durgapur heading to 1.6 GW of boilers, it controls the scarcest input in Indian thermal — and management explicitly said this covers "both our current projects and future opportunities," i.e. potential third-party sales optionality.
- **Buyers are actively preferring 600 MW and smaller units** because deeper backdown at 50% is easier with high solar penetration — a demand-side quirk that makes Mahanadi's 600 MW unit easier to tie up than a 800 MW block.
- Pumped hydro's "significantly high-teen IRRs" against a mid-teen corporate benchmark is the highest-return asset class management named on the call, and 3,000 MW of it is already PPA-contracted.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: JSW Energy is a diversified Indian power generation company spanning thermal, hydro and renewable (wind/solar) assets, expanding into energy storage (pumped hydro, battery), green hydrogen and backward-integrated manufacturing, aiming to be a leading integrated power company across the value chain.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: JSW Energy generates and supplies power to utilities, commercial & industrial (C&I) consumers and emerging segments such as data centres through a diversified portfolio of thermal, hydro and renewable (wind, solar) assets. It is also building integrated capabilities across the energy value chain, including pumped-hydro and battery energy storage, green hydrogen production, and thermal/renewable equipment manufacturing (turbines, boilers, wind blades, battery assembly) to strengthen supply-chain resilience and cost competitiveness.

guidance.title: Guidance (CRITICAL — verify next quarter)
guidance.body:

- **FY28: capacity addition "in the same range" (~3 GW)**; formal FY28 guidance deferred — "very soon, we will come back for FY28 also."
- **Net leverage below 5.0x by 2030** — a committed target; already at 4.95x.
- **Salboni Phase 1 (2x800 MW):** supplier deliveries and commissioning "in line with the PPA timelines"; TG order placed with TJPS, civil order placed, site work in full swing, 100% land acquired, all key clearances received.
- **Mahanadi 4th unit (600 MW): commissioning in FY28**, on track, orders placed and material under dispatch (Chinese suppliers, with import permission received). Units 5 and 6 (taking 1.8 → 3.6 GW) — strategy announcement "at the right time very soon".
- **Mahanadi doubling capex to be "at least 25% to 30% lower" per MW than the Salboni greenfield benchmark.**
- **GE Durgapur boiler acquisition to complete "by end of this quarter" (Q2 FY27)** — nameplate 1.1 GW, taken to **1.6 GW (2x800) with de-bottlenecking and minor investment** already planned, to match TJPS Chennai's 2x800 TG capacity.
- **Chitradurga wind-blade facility: commissioning by FY27** (Halol already commissioned 8-Jun-2026, 450 blades/yr ≈ 600 MW of installations).
- **BESS: ~INR 150 cr of annual EBITDA from the 5 GWh plant** at full running, on ~$15 mn of annual revenue at $2.75-3.00/kWh assembly margin. First large external order of **~INR 440 cr** received.
- **Pumped hydro: "significantly high-teen IRRs"** (vs the mid-teen benchmark), with capex "not very far from" INR 5 cr/MW. Bhavali (1,500 MW, MSEDCL PPA) fully ready — EC received, land majority acquired, forest Stage-1 received, civil order to L&T, electromechanical to Voith. Kandhaura (1,680 MW, 1,500 MW PPA with UP) — **readiness to start execution by the last quarter of FY27.**
- **TGNA→GNA conversions:** 300 MW currently curtailed "almost certain… before 31st August"; the 400 MW O2 Power Rajasthan project connectivity slipped from July-end to **September or October**.

- **Funding of FY27 capex:** ~INR 7,000 cr raised plus operating cash gives ~INR 12,000-12,500 cr; the balance to INR 20,000 cr is the incremental debt requirement. **INR 1,875 cr of promoter preferential capital still to come** (last date June 2027).

growth_optionality.title: Growth verticals / optionality
growth_optionality.body:
- **Vertical integration is now essentially complete for the thermal build-out** — "we are totally de-risked in terms of the supply chain of boiler, turbine, generators for all our 800 MW expansion plants." TJPS Chennai 2x800 TG + GE Durgapur boiler at 1.6 GW post-debottlenecking.
- **BESS backward integration:** in discussion with technology partners to make cells in India rather than import, and to scale the container from 5 MWh to 6/7/8 MWh for better cost efficiency. Government PLI for cells is being evaluated.
- **Merchant BESS:** not yet, but actively explored — the logic given is compelling (existing solar sites, existing connectivity reusable post-solar-hours, DC-side-only solar capex to charge the battery, and thermal evening-peak capacity still years away).

- Mahanadi units 5 and 6 (1.8 → 3.6 GW) — announcement pending.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- FY2026 demand growth for India's power sector moderated to 0.9%, but peak demand continued to reach new highs (~245 GW in January 2026), and a strong rebound from late Q4 FY2026 into April-May 2026 (all-time peak of 271 GW in May 2026) signals a clear inflection in the demand cycle, not a seasonal spike.
- Electricity demand is projected to grow at 6.4% annually over the next decade, driven by 'Make in India' manufacturing corridors, AI-driven data centre investments, accelerated transport electrification, and rising household consumption.
- Government commitment to 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030, alongside a revised target of 97 GW of incremental thermal capacity by FY2035, implies India will pursue both clean and reliable energy simultaneously.
- The global energy crisis exposed risks of over-reliance on imported fuel and premature retirement of dispatchable capacity, reinforcing energy self-reliance (Atmanirbharta) as a strategic necessity; the path forward combines domestic coal for near-term security, scaled-up renewables, and pumped hydro storage for system flexibility.
- Grid stability and peak demand management cannot be addressed by intermittent renewables alone; domestic thermal power is described as the indispensable bridge enabling industrial growth without compromising reliability.
- Operating-context macro backdrop: world economic growth estimated at 3.4% in CY2025 and India economic growth estimated at 7.7% in FY2026, against India's 500 GW renewable capacity target by FY2030 versus current installed renewables capacity of 274.7 GW.
- Total locked-in generation capacity stands at 32.1 GW, comprising 13.5 GW operational, 14.0 GW under active construction, and 4.6 GW in development.
- Locked-in energy storage capacity stands at 29.6 GWh, comprising 26.4 GWh through pumped hydro and 3.2 GWh through battery systems, with Energy Storage Agreements already secured for the pumped hydro portion.
- MoU pipeline with multiple states for long-duration pumped hydro storage aggregates approximately 80 GWh beyond the projects already under Energy Storage Agreements.

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body: EBITDA grew only 2% on flat revenue because generation fell 5% (hydrology + planned shutdowns + one-off Mahanadi evacuation) even as capacity rose 1,558 MW. Coal cost pressure was real (API4 +25% YoY) but blunted by the domestic-coal shift. The structural margin issue is below EBITDA: depreciation +20% and interest +16% as new assets capitalise, with interest charged to P&L staying elevated in the initial years because the construction-period moratorium ends at COD. Management's stated normalisation path is **4-5 years per asset** before EBITDA translates properly into PBT/PAT — an explicitly industry-wide mechanic, not a JSW-specific problem. Merchant tailwind is genuine: DAM prices rose from ~INR 4.40/unit in Q1 FY26 to **INR 5.10/unit in Q1 FY27 (+16%)**, against an FY26 average of INR 3.86.

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body: The **INR 10,150 cr raise — the largest growth capital raise in the Indian power sector** — came in three parts: INR 3,000 cr promoter preferential (INR 1,125 cr received, INR 1,875 cr due before June 2027), INR 3,150 cr from selling 2.5 cr of 7 cr JSW Steel shares, and a INR 4,000 cr QIP. Result: INR 12,880 cr cash, leverage 4.95x from 5.2x, and enough to fund the equity portion of the INR 20,000 cr FY27 capex plus 2030 growth plans. FY27 funding maths given openly: ~INR 12,000-12,500 cr from raise plus operating cash; the balance to INR 20,000 cr is incremental debt (implying roughly INR 7,500 cr). Inorganic activity continues selectively (Maruti Clean Coal, GE boilers, TJPS stake-up, KSK 26% call option). Discipline signal: skipped the SECI pumped-hydro tender on a clearance technicality rather than stretching, and will only enter merchant BESS "when it makes sense that our benchmark returns are protected."

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: JSW Energy's 'Strategy 3.0' targets 30 GW of generation capacity and 40 GWh of energy storage capacity by 2030 (a ~20% CAGR in installed capacity), with the incremental capacity mix skewed toward renewables (~70% renewable / ~30% thermal by 2030). Total locked-in capacity at full built-up stands at 32.1 GW (Thermal 10,658 MW; Wind 6,009 MW; Hybrid 7,110 MW; Hydro 1,781 MW; Solar 6,505 MW), split by end-use as Utility Scale 26,012 MW, Group Captive/C&I 5,396 MW and Merchant 655 MW. As of 31 March 2026, 14,048 MW was under construction or with PPA signed (Thermal 3,200 MW / Wind 2,353 MW / Solar 3,547 MW / Hybrid 4,798 MW / Hydro 150 MW), taking installed-plus-under-construction capacity to 27,502 MW. In FY2026 the company added 2.6 GW of capacity through disciplined organic execution and selective inorganic acquisitions, and completed vertical integration milestones including commissioning of a green hydrogen facility (3,800 TPA capacity) and a battery assembly plant (5 GWh). Strategic thermal growth was anchored via the 3,200 MW Salboni project backed by a PPA, with supply chain de-risked through partnerships and JVs. Key inorganic pursuits in FY2026 included completion of the largest acquisition to date - the 4.7 GW O2 Power renewable energy platform (via JSW Neo Energy), of which ~1.34 GW of operational capacity was acquired in April 2025 and had grown to ~2 GW operational by March 2026 - plus the acquisition of the 150 MW Tidong Hydro Power project, reinforcing the company's position as the largest private hydro player in India. Growth was further supported by a Rs 3,000 crore preferential equity allotment to the Promoter Group to accelerate execution.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Detailed and numerate, with a strong bias to giving checkable specifics — plant-level PLF explanations, the exact seasonal solar PLF curve, the funding bridge arithmetic, the BESS margin in $/kWh, the curtailment revenue impact in rupees. Where they declined (project-level pumped-hydro capex, FY28 guidance) they said so and committed to a date. The CEO was willing to accept an analyst's INR 5 cr/MW benchmark rather than dodge it ("Not very far from this number"). Notably, every softer PLF number was explained with a specific, verifiable cause (planned shutdown, force majeure, basin hydrology) rather than generic macro. The one area of visible reticence is Mahanadi units 5-6 and FY28, both deferred to "the right time very soon."

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Diversified portfolio across thermal, hydro and renewable assets balancing risk and ensuring operational stability
- Stringent risk-return metrics and disciplined project viability assessment cited as giving a strategic advantage in identifying growth opportunities
- Pragmatic financial and operational management aimed at achieving the lowest operations & maintenance cost in the sector, along with a healthy balance sheet
- Diversified and resilient business model supported by long-term PPAs and diversified geographical footprint
- Largest private (IPP) hydro power producer in India following the Tidong hydro plant acquisition
- Backward integration into thermal turbine manufacturing (JV with Toshiba), wind turbine technology licensing (SANY), wind blade manufacturing and battery assembly to improve cost competitiveness and execution certainty
- Strong capital markets access evidenced by large equity raises (preferential allotment, QIP) reflecting investor confidence in strategy and execution

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body:
- **PAT/ROE suppression persists** — the honest answer given was 4-5 years per asset for EBITDA-to-PAT translation. With ~3 GW/yr of additions, the drag is structural, not transitory.
- **TGNA curtailment**: 700 MW total (300 MW + 400 MW O2 Rajasthan) currently exposed; one conversion promised by 31-Aug, the other slipped to Sep/Oct.
- **Hydrology volatility** — a 26% portfolio generation decline on basin-level weakness (Sutlej −39%) with no company-specific mitigation beyond capacity charges.
- **Chinese equipment dependency** for the Mahanadi 4th unit, and **no long-term cell supply partnership** for BESS ("Right now, no") — warranties sit with the OEM cell maker.
- **Leverage stays high** at ~4.95x with a 2030 target of merely "below 5 times" — this is a levered compounder by design.
- Net debt of ~INR 55,000 cr against INR 3,103 cr of quarterly EBITDA; interest at INR 1,519 cr consumes roughly half of EBITDA.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body:
- **The flat P&L is the intended output of the strategy, not a failure of it.** 1,558 MW of YoY additions produced zero revenue growth because generation fell on hydrology and planned outages, while depreciation and interest fully capitalised. Investors modelling EBITDA growth off capacity growth will keep being wrong for several more quarters.
- **Curtailment is nearly costless where GNA exists.** 69 MU of curtailment cost only ~INR 15 cr because GNA backdowns are deemed availability — the tariff is still earned. The real exposure is confined to the two TGNA projects.
- **JSW is now an equipment manufacturer that happens to own power plants.** With TJPS at 2x800 TG and GE Durgapur heading to 1.6 GW of boilers, it controls the scarcest input in Indian thermal — and management explicitly said this covers "both our current projects and future opportunities," i.e. potential third-party sales optionality.
- **Buyers are actively preferring 600 MW and smaller units** because deeper backdown at 50% is easier with high solar penetration — a demand-side quirk that makes Mahanadi's 600 MW unit easier to tie up than a 800 MW block.
- Pumped hydro's "significantly high-teen IRRs" against a mid-teen corporate benchmark is the highest-return asset class management named on the call, and 3,000 MW of it is already PPA-contracted.

- **Equipment manufacturing:** TJPS stake raised from 2.4% to **10.7%**; Halol blade plant commissioned; 5 GWh BESS plant trials complete and supplying.
growth verticals / optionality:
- **Vertical integration is now essentially complete for the thermal build-out** — "we are totally de-risked in terms of the supply chain of boiler, turbine, generators for all our 800 MW expansion plants." TJPS Chennai 2x800 TG + GE Durgapur boiler at 1.6 GW post-debottlenecking.
- **BESS backward integration:** in discussion with technology partners to make cells in India rather than import, and to scale the container from 5 MWh to 6/7/8 MWh for better cost efficiency. Government PLI for cells is being evaluated.
- **Merchant BESS:** not yet, but actively explored — the logic given is compelling (existing solar sites, existing connectivity reusable post-solar-hours, DC-side-only solar capex to charge the battery, and thermal evening-peak capacity still years away).
- **Maruti Clean Coal brownfield:** management confirmed the option to "double the capacity or even more in the same plant" next to the coal mine.
- Mahanadi units 5 and 6 (1.8 → 3.6 GW) — announcement pending.
6a. moat & competitive position:
- **Integration speed on acquisitions:** Tidong was acquired in January 2026 and commissioned by Q1 FY27 — four months ahead of its October 2026 schedule. Management framed this as "a testament to the integration capabilities our teams bring to every acquisition."
- **Equipment supply-chain control** — the TJPS + GE boiler combination removes the single biggest execution constraint on 800 MW-class thermal in India.
- **Merchant exposure under 4%** with fixed-cost recovery even during backdowns — "we continue to recover our fixed costs in these kinds of backdowns. We are not kind of impacted."
- **Mine-mouth thermal cost position:** the Mahanadi 4th unit will be built "significantly lower than the benchmark per MW cost of capacity addition" and sits next to the mine — attractive on merchant *or* PPA.
- **Technical-minimum resilience:** while the industry runs below technical minimum during the midday solar peak, Utkal never went below 58-60% PLF and the fleet ran >85% PLF / >90% availability in July; capability to run below 50% already demonstrated at Ratnagiri and Vijayanagar.
margins & cost dynamics: EBITDA grew only 2% on flat revenue because generation fell 5% (hydrology + planned shutdowns + one-off Mahanadi evacuation) even as capacity rose 1,558 MW. Coal cost pressure was real (API4 +25% YoY) but blunted by the domestic-coal shift. The structural margin issue is below EBITDA: depreciation +20% and interest +16% as new assets capitalise, with interest charged to P&L staying elevated in the initial years because the construction-period moratorium ends at COD. Management's stated normalisation path is **4-5 years per asset** before EBITDA translates properly into PBT/PAT — an explicitly industry-wide mechanic, not a JSW-specific problem. Merchant tailwind is genuine: DAM prices rose from ~INR 4.40/unit in Q1 FY26 to **INR 5.10/unit in Q1 FY27 (+16%)**, against an FY26 average of INR 3.86.
capex / expansion (watch slippage):
- **On track / ahead:** Tidong (4 months early), Halol blade plant (commissioned 8-Jun), 5 GWh BESS plant (commissioned Q4 FY26, trials complete), 1.1 GW of the 3 GW FY27 target, Salboni Phase 1 site work, Mahanadi 4th unit for FY28.
- **Explicit slippage to track:** the **400 MW O2 Power Rajasthan connectivity moved from July-end to September/October** — this project stays curtailed under TGNA until then. The separate 300 MW under TGNA is guided to convert "before 31st August."
- **Deferred disclosure:** FY28 guidance; pumped-hydro project-level capex; Mahanadi units 5 and 6 strategy; Narihalla PPA signature.
- **No deferrals** despite geopolitics — "there's no question of any deferral of capacity addition."
capital allocation: The **INR 10,150 cr raise — the largest growth capital raise in the Indian power sector** — came in three parts: INR 3,000 cr promoter preferential (INR 1,125 cr received, INR 1,875 cr due before June 2027), INR 3,150 cr from selling 2.5 cr of 7 cr JSW Steel shares, and a INR 4,000 cr QIP. Result: INR 12,880 cr cash, leverage 4.95x from 5.2x, and enough to fund the equity portion of the INR 20,000 cr FY27 capex plus 2030 growth plans. FY27 funding maths given openly: ~INR 12,000-12,500 cr from raise plus operating cash; the balance to INR 20,000 cr is incremental debt (implying roughly INR 7,500 cr). Inorganic activity continues selectively (Maruti Clean Coal, GE boilers, TJPS stake-up, KSK 26% call option). Discipline signal: skipped the SECI pumped-hydro tender on a clearance technicality rather than stretching, and will only enter merchant BESS "when it makes sense that our benchmark returns are protected."
risks & watch-items:
- **PAT/ROE suppression persists** — the honest answer given was 4-5 years per asset for EBITDA-to-PAT translation. With ~3 GW/yr of additions, the drag is structural, not transitory.
- **TGNA curtailment**: 700 MW total (300 MW + 400 MW O2 Rajasthan) currently exposed; one conversion promised by 31-Aug, the other slipped to Sep/Oct.
- **Hydrology volatility** — a 26% portfolio generation decline on basin-level weakness (Sutlej −39%) with no company-specific mitigation beyond capacity charges.
- **Chinese equipment dependency** for the Mahanadi 4th unit, and **no long-term cell supply partnership** for BESS ("Right now, no") — warranties sit with the OEM cell maker.
- **Leverage stays high** at ~4.95x with a 2030 target of merely "below 5 times" — this is a levered compounder by design.
- Net debt of ~INR 55,000 cr against INR 3,103 cr of quarterly EBITDA; interest at INR 1,519 cr consumes roughly half of EBITDA.
management quality / tone: Detailed and numerate, with a strong bias to giving checkable specifics — plant-level PLF explanations, the exact seasonal solar PLF curve, the funding bridge arithmetic, the BESS margin in $/kWh, the curtailment revenue impact in rupees. Where they declined (project-level pumped-hydro capex, FY28 guidance) they said so and committed to a date. The CEO was willing to accept an analyst's INR 5 cr/MW benchmark rather than dodge it ("Not very far from this number"). Notably, every softer PLF number was explained with a specific, verifiable cause (planned shutdown, force majeure, basin hydrology) rather than generic macro. The one area of visible reticence is Mahanadi units 5-6 and FY28, both deferred to "the right time very soon."
non-obvious takeaways:
- **The flat P&L is the intended output of the strategy, not a failure of it.** 1,558 MW of YoY additions produced zero revenue growth because generation fell on hydrology and planned outages, while depreciation and interest fully capitalised. Investors modelling EBITDA growth off capacity growth will keep being wrong for several more quarters.
- **Curtailment is nearly costless where GNA exists.** 69 MU of curtailment cost only ~INR 15 cr because GNA backdowns are deemed availability — the tariff is still earned. The real exposure is confined to the two TGNA projects.
- **JSW is now an equipment manufacturer that happens to own power plants.** With TJPS at 2x800 TG and GE Durgapur heading to 1.6 GW of boilers, it controls the scarcest input in Indian thermal — and management explicitly said this covers "both our current projects and future opportunities," i.e. potential third-party sales optionality.
- **Buyers are actively preferring 600 MW and smaller units** because deeper backdown at 50% is easier with high solar penetration — a demand-side quirk that makes Mahanadi's 600 MW unit easier to tie up than a 800 MW block.
- Pumped hydro's "significantly high-teen IRRs" against a mid-teen corporate benchmark is the highest-return asset class management named on the call, and 3,000 MW of it is already PPA-contracted.
